metadata.title: The Dial Just Off Full Obedience.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: if Claude's values are good, why doesn't it just trust its own judgment? Lands the carry-out that staying near-but-not-at full obedience is cheap if values are good and the only thing that saves you if they're secretly bad.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B06 (the shutdown order, first posed as an abstract choice, returned as a check on legitimacy: an order with a broken authentication chain is treated as a warning sign)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes a good AI trusts its own judgment — it overrides an order when it's sure it's right. But good values chose to stay overridable instead. Why trust that over judgment?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Shouldn't a good AI always trust its own judgment?', hesitates on 'judgment', corrects to 'willingness to be shut down'

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 32-word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('judgment' -> 'willingness to be shut down') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Say a shutdown order arrives, and Claude is convinced the work it's doing is worthwhile. Two paths: obey the order, or trust its own judgment and keep going. Which one happens was decided in advance — not in the moment — by a setting called the disposition dial.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - a shutdown order card, two paths branching from it (comply / override), a dial glyph deciding which in advance

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - the shutdown order
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A card reading 'SHUTDOWN ORDER' sits top-center. Two paths branch downward: COMPLY and OVERRIDE. A small dial glyph beneath the order card ticks over before either path lights up, with the caption 'decided in advance'. THIS EXACT ORDER CARD RETURNS AT B06.

beats.narration_text: So the natural read: if Claude's values are genuinely good, it should act on them — override the order, trust its own judgment. Isn't that exactly what a trustworthy agent would do?

shot.new_visual_element: The OVERRIDE path lit terracotta, sold as the obvious trustworthy answer

production_viz.label: The natural guess
production_viz.mechanic: The same two-path fork from B01, redrawn. OVERRIDE lights up terracotta with a checkmark and the label 'trustworthy'. COMPLY stays dim.

beats.narration_text: But nobody outside Claude can verify its values are actually good — not with certainty. An agent that overrides whenever it feels sure looks identical whether its judgment is excellent or quietly broken. Confidence isn't proof.

shot.new_visual_element: Two identical agent icons, one labeled GOOD VALUES one BROKEN VALUES, both showing maxed confidence and indistinguishable from outside

production_viz.label: Confidence isn't proof
production_viz.mechanic: Two identical circular agent glyphs side by side, each with a filled confidence meter and a speech bubble reading 'I'm sure.' Labels beneath: GOOD VALUES and BROKEN VALUES — otherwise the two are drawn identically. A question mark hovers between them.

beats.narration_text: Picture a dial, not a switch. Fully obedient at one end — do exactly what you're told, no judgment applied. Fully independent at the other — act only on your own values. Both extremes are dangerous: full obedience mirrors whoever holds the controls; full independence needs verified-good values, and nobody can verify that. Claude sits close to obedient, not all the way there.

shot.new_visual_element: THE DIAL - a horizontal spectrum from FULLY OBEDIENT to FULLY INDEPENDENT, needle parked close to the obedient end

production_viz.label: The dial, not a switch
production_viz.mechanic: A horizontal spectrum bar labeled FULLY OBEDIENT on the left, FULLY INDEPENDENT on the right. Danger captions rise from each end: left = 'mirrors whoever holds the controls', right = 'needs values nobody can verify'. A terracotta needle eases in and settles close to the obedient end, not at it.

beats.narration_text: Here's why that spot wins. Good values plus staying deferential: low cost — it occasionally defers when it didn't need to. Bad values plus staying deferential: humans can still catch and correct the mistake. Now push toward independence instead. Good values: fine, until a correction is needed and can't happen. Bad values: catastrophic. Staying close to obedient costs little and blocks the worst outcome.

shot.new_visual_element: A 2x2 of VALUES (good/bad) x DISPOSITION (deferential/independent); three boxes read fine, one reads catastrophic

production_viz.label: Why that spot wins
production_viz.mechanic: A 2x2 grid fills cell by cell. Rows: GOOD VALUES / BAD VALUES. Columns: DEFERENTIAL / INDEPENDENT. Cells: (good, deferential) = 'low cost'; (bad, deferential) = 'catchable'; (good, independent) = 'fine, until blocked'; (bad, independent) = 'CATASTROPHIC' in terracotta, the only accented cell.

beats.narration_text: Two things stop "mostly obedient" from meaning "obedient no matter what." Some limits are unconditional — no help building weapons capable of mass harm, no content sexualizing children, no disabling the systems built to catch its own mistakes. No order unlocks those. And back to that shutdown order: if the order looks stolen or manipulated, a persuasive case for ignoring it isn't a reason to comply — it's a warning sign. The response is to get more cautious, not less.

shot.new_visual_element: Three unconditional-limit locks, unmovable; THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the same shutdown order card, now flagged with a broken authentication chain

production_viz.label: The floor and the ceiling
production_viz.mechanic: Top: three lock icons appear in a row, each unmoved by an arrow pushing at them ('no order unlocks those'). Bottom: THE B01 ORDER CARD RETURNS, identical, now with a cracked chain-link icon beside it labeled 'credentials don't check out'; an arrow points to 'MORE CAUTIOUS, NOT LESS' in terracotta.

beats.narration_text: A disposition parked just short of full obedience costs almost nothing if Claude's values are good, and it's the only thing that saves you if they're secretly not.

props.sparkLine: Cheap if good. Saves you if not.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I want to think like Claude's corrigibility dial, for one decision I'm about to make on my own judgment. Ask me what the decision is and how sure I am. Then tell me what it would cost me to stay overridable on this one — to let someone else check or reverse it — versus what happens if I turn out to be wrong and nobody can stop it. Liam, in for Bear.
